demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
Being superalert or watchful or on guard
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, a specific sense of danger from strangers is hard to reconcile unless there is additional trauma history not represented here. The other threat items reflect generalized hypervigilance, but this item implies an interpersonal-danger context that is not supported by the trauma type or by any trigger, memory, appraisal, or strategy items.

issues.item: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, this threat profile is hard to reconcile clinically: all selected items imply persistent fear of immediate external physical danger, which fits assault/combat more than bereavement trauma. In isolation, bereavement-related PTSD can involve arousal, but a purely danger-scanning threat node without any accompanying memory, trigger, appraisal, or strategy content linking the threat to reminders of the loved one's death is not coherent here. This is also difficult to square with the formulation, which specifies no active edges; the threat items strongly imply linkage to triggers or trauma reminders, yet no such connected content is present.

vignette:
Linh Tran is a 31-year-old Vietnamese-American journalist, recently divorced, who presented for an initial intake following the sudden death of her younger brother Minh eight months ago. Minh, who was 27, collapsed without warning at a family gathering - a cerebral aneurysm, the coroner later confirmed, that killed him within minutes before an ambulance could arrive. Linh had been the one standing closest to him when he fell. She held his head in her lap on the kitchen floor of their parents' home in San Jose, speaking to him, watching his face change, not understanding at first and then understanding completely. There was no violence, no threat she could have anticipated or defended against - only the sudden, absolute subtraction of someone who had been entirely alive seconds before. That unanswerability became the wound she could not close.

In the weeks following Minh's death, Linh found that her nervous system had quietly reorganised itself around a single premise: that catastrophe could arrive without signal, at any moment, in any ordinary place. A kitchen. A Sunday afternoon. A person laughing. She had come to believe, not as an intellectual position but as something closer to bodily knowledge, that safety was a story people told themselves - and that she had simply stopped being able to tell it. The result was a state of near-constant vigilance that she could neither justify to others nor switch off in herself. She scanned rooms when she entered them. She watched the faces of people she loved for signs of something going wrong. At family dinners, which she now attended with a kind of dread, she found herself monitoring her parents' colour, their breathing, the way they moved, alert to any deviation from the ordinary. She could not name what she was watching for, exactly - only that she was always watching.

Her work as a journalist, which had once felt like a natural expression of her curiosity and drive, had become one of the primary arenas in which this vigilance played out. Linh covers local politics and community affairs for a mid-sized Bay Area outlet, and her days involve interviews, press briefings, and long hours at her desk or in the field. She had noticed, over the months since Minh's death, that she could no longer sit through a briefing without her attention fragmenting - one part of her tracking the speaker, another part sweeping the room, cataloguing exits, assessing who looked unwell, who was pale, who was holding their head in a way that seemed wrong. Colleagues had begun to comment, gently at first and then with more concern, that she seemed distracted, that her copy had grown thinner. Her editor, who knew about Minh, had offered her leave. She had declined, believing that stopping would be worse - that work was the one structure holding the rest of her together. That belief had cost her a feature assignment she had been developing for months, reassigned quietly while she was on a deadline she had missed.

The emotional texture of her days was one of relentless, exhausting intensity. She described strong surges of fear that arrived without clear provocation - sitting at her laptop, waiting at a crosswalk, lying in bed in the apartment she had moved into after her divorce finalised last year. Alongside the fear was something she struggled to name: a compound of horror and guilt and a rage she found shameful, directed at no one in particular and at herself most of all, for having been unable to do anything, for having simply held him and waited. She had not relaxed, she said - not once, not fully - since the afternoon he died. Even in moments she recognised as objectively safe, her body refused the information. Sleep was shallow and easily broken. Stillness felt dangerous, as though vigilance itself were the only thing standing between her and the next unbearable thing.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a conversation with her mother, who told her, with quiet devastation, that being around Linh now felt frightening - that her watchfulness had begun to make everyone around her feel as though something terrible was always about to happen. Linh had cried in her car afterwards for a long time. What she most hoped for, she said at intake, was to be able to sit in a room with the people she loved without waiting for one of them to disappear.
